summary.text: A camera is an instrument that captures and stores images and video, either digitally with an electronic sensor or chemically on light-sensitive film.
Its main parts are exposure control, a lens that focuses the light, a viewfinder to preview the scene, and the film or sensor that records it.
Cameras grew from the camera obscura through 19th-century pioneers to digital models, which outsold film cameras in the United States by 2003, and then to smartphones.

items.prompt: A photo comes out too dark because too little light reached the sensor. Which camera part is meant to regulate that?
items.explain: Exposure control regulates the amount of light reaching the sensor or film.

items.prompt: Which camera part lets the photographer preview the scene before pressing the button?
items.explain: The viewfinder allows the user to preview the scene, while the lens focuses light and the film or sensor captures it.

items.prompt: A photographer wants to see, in real time, exactly what the lens sees. Which type of camera provides that?
items.explain: Single-lens reflex cameras provide real-time, exact imaging through the lens, unlike rangefinders, which have separate viewing and imaging systems.

items.prompt: In the late 1800s dry plates and roll-film arrived. What shift did they prompt?

options.label: Toward larger and more expensive cameras
Toward cameras that only worked in studios
Toward cameras without any lens at all
Toward smaller and more cost-effective cameras

items.explain: These advances pushed designs toward smaller, cheaper cameras, as shown by the original Kodak.

items.prompt: Why has the smartphone blurred the line between cameras and other devices?

options.label: It is easy to use, so dedicated cameras compete with a multifunctional device
It produces larger film negatives than other cameras
It replaced the lens with a pinhole
It cannot record video and so is not a camera

items.explain: Smartphone cameras are easier to use and blur the lines between dedicated cameras and multifunctional devices.

items.prompt: After World War I, which country took the lead in camera development, with precision-made cameras?

options.label: The USSR, with copied Western designs
The UK, with pocket film cameras

items.explain: Germany led after World War I, consolidating the industry and producing precision-made cameras such as the Leica and Contax.

paragraphs.heading: What a camera is
paragraphs.text: A camera is an instrument for capturing and storing pictures and video. It records them in one of two ways: digitally, with an electronic image sensor, or chemically, on a light-sensitive material such as photographic film. As the core tool of photography and videography, the camera has shaped the visual arts, media, entertainment, surveillance and scientific research.

paragraphs.heading: The basic design
paragraphs.text: Every camera follows the same basic plan. Light enters a closed box through a converging, or convex, lens, and the image is recorded on a light-sensitive medium. A shutter controls how long the light is let in. Most cameras also have a viewfinder that shows the scene to be recorded, plus ways to adjust focus, aperture and shutter speed. Most capture visible light, but specialised cameras record other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, such as infrared.

paragraphs.heading: Aperture and f-stops
paragraphs.text: The aperture is the opening that lets light in, usually located in the lens and adjusted by overlapping plates. Widening or narrowing it changes how much light reaches the film or sensor. It moves in standard steps called f-stops, typically from f/1.4 through f/2, f/2.8 and f/4 and on up to f/32. A lower f-stop means a wider opening and more light, and each step up halves the light that gets in.

paragraphs.heading: Depth of field
paragraphs.text: The aperture also controls how much of the scene looks sharp. At a low f-stop the wide opening narrows the range of focus, so the foreground can be crisp while the background blurs. This range of sharpness, called depth of field, grows as the aperture closes.

paragraphs.heading: Nineteenth-century beginnings
paragraphs.text: The camera grew out of the camera obscura in the 19th century, through pioneers such as Thomas Wedgwood, Nicéphore Niépce and Henry Fox Talbot. They first used the camera obscura for chemical experiments, then built cameras made for chemical photography, and later shrank them and improved their lenses. The daguerreotype process, introduced in 1839, opened the way to commercial camera making, and by the 1850s it was a specialised trade with standard designs and sizes. Dry plates and roll film then brought smaller, cheaper cameras, such as the original Kodak of 1888.

paragraphs.heading: Digital and the smartphone
paragraphs.text: Digital photography took over at the end of the 20th century, and in the United States digital cameras were outselling film cameras by 2003. Building cameras into smartphones then made taking photos an everyday activity. This century also saw computational photography take off, using algorithms and AI to improve pictures. Phone cameras now commonly offer low-light and HDR modes, optical image stabilisation and depth sensing. Because a phone camera is easier to use, it has blurred the line between dedicated cameras and devices that do many things.
